algebra__L08.md.fix: Insert an intermediate step, e.g. 'square-root both sides: x + 3 = √7, so x = −3 + √7; matching −3 + √k gives k =' before the final box.

algebra__L13.md.why: The three boxes the student has just filled are 16, 8 and 4 (the whole terms in quarters). The final sum then reads '28 + 2 + 1' — but none of those three numbers matches the boxes just computed. 28 is an unnamed running subtotal (16+8+4) that was never shown as a step, and the 2 and 1 are the 1/2 and 1/4 terms converted into quarters — a conversion the walk never builds (the intro only lists the raw fractions 1/2, 1/4). A struggling student who has typed 16, 8, 4 will stare at '28 + 2 + 1' with no idea where any of the three numbers came from.
algebra__L13.md.fix: Add explicit conversion asks for the fractional terms and name the subtotal, e.g. 'Half in quarters: 1/2 = [box=2]', 'Quarter in quarters: 1/4 = [box=1]', then 'Add the whole parts: 16 + 8 + 4 = [box=28]', then 'Total quarters: 28 + 2 + 1 = [box=31]'.

algebra__L13.md.step: First gap is 8 - k; second gap is (2k + 1) - 8 = 2k - 7. Set 8 - k = 2k - 7, add k to both sides: 8 = 3k - 7. Add 7: 3k =  [box=15]

A struggling 15-year-old has to re-read the whole line to locate what '3k = ' actually depends on, and any slip in the reasoning above is invisible because there is no box to check it against.
algebra__L13.md.fix: Break it into staged asks with their own boxes: 'Second gap: (2k + 1) - 8 = 2k - [box=7]', then 'Set the gaps equal: 8 - k = 2k - 7. Add k to both sides: 8 = 3k - [box=7]', then 'Add 7 to both sides: 3k = [box=15]'.

It is also a check that quietly invokes the 'middle term × number of terms' shortcut, so the phrasing is the only thing anchoring it.
algebra__L13.md.fix: Rewrite as: "Check: the middle term (7) times the number of terms (5): 7 × 5 ="

The student cannot see where 32 comes from, and the method contradicts the step-by-step halving used two lines later.

algebra__L13.md.why: "Zero term" is technical jargon introduced with no explanation of what it is or why you subtract the common difference from the first term. A struggling student can do the sum 4 − 5 but has no idea what they just built or why it works.
algebra__L13.md.fix: Introduce it in plain words the first time, e.g. "The term that would sit before the 1st one (the 0th term): first term − common difference = 4 − 5 =". Then "Add the zero term" makes sense on later lines.

algebra__L13.md.step: The 5n part of the 10th term: 5 × 10 =  [box=50, NO label]

algebra__L13.md.fix: Add a stating line before the jump: "So the rule is 5n − 1. Now, for n = 10, the 5n part is 5 × 10 =".

algebra__L13.md.step: Check nothing smaller is shared: is 7 in the second list? 3m + 2 = 7 gives 3m =  [box=5, NO label]

algebra__L05.md.step: Cross multiply: the left top times 2, the right top times 5. Left: 2 × 2(x − 1) = 4(x − 1). Expand the left: 4 × (−1) =

The notation '2 × 2(x − 1)' uses two different 2s (the cross-multiply factor and the coefficient inside the bracket), which is easy to misread; the student then has to spot that the 4 they multiply came from '2 × 2'.
algebra__L05.md.fix: Split it up. Say separately: 'The left top is 2(x − 1); multiply it by 2 to get 4(x − 1).' Then ask on its own short line: 'Expand: 4 × (−1) ='.

algebra__L05.md.step: Cross-multiply. Left numerator times 4 gives 16x − 12. Right numerator times 5: 5 × 3x = [box=15, label:'x']

number__L04.md.step: Check it is a multiple of the first number: 22680 ÷ 360 =  [box=63, NO label]

A struggling student following the steps has no idea where 360 came from, so the final check step is unfollowable.

number__L04.md.step: Shared power of 2, the lower of 2 and 2, is  [box=2, NO label]
number__L04.md.why: Three identical digits collide in one clause: the prime (2), both exponents being compared (2 and 2), and the answer (2). A struggling reader cannot tell which '2' is the prime and which are the powers. It is compounded by the phrase 'power of 2', which a 15-year-old idiomatically reads as a VALUE like 4 or 8 (2-to-a-power), not 'the exponent sitting on the prime 2' — so it is unclear whether the box wants the exponent or 2^exponent. The same ambiguous 'Shared power of N, the lower of A and B' construction recurs where the prime digit sits next to an equal exponent digit: bronze[1] and bronze[6] ('power of 2, the lower of 2 and 1'), and gold[0] ('power of 2, the lower of 4 and 2'). Non-colliding cases (e.g. 'Shared power of 3, the lower of 1 and 2') read more cleanly but still use the ambiguous 'power of' wording.
number__L04.md.fix: Name the prime and the quantity wanted explicitly, separating them from the digits, e.g. 'The prime 2 is in both numbers. Take the SMALLER exponent — the lower of 2 and 2 = ___'. Apply the same rewrite to every 'Shared power of N' step (bronze[1], bronze[6], silver[1], silver[3], gold[0]).

number__L04.md.why: The word 'power' is used to mean two different things across the lesson. In silver[0] 'The power of 2 in 48 is [4]' the box wants the exponent (4). Here — and in silver[3] '3² = [9]', silver[5] '2² = [4]', gold[0], gold[4] — 'Lowest/highest power of X is Xⁿ = [ ]' wants the computed value (2¹ = 2), not the exponent. A student who learned from silver[0] that 'power' is the small number would type 1 here and be marked wrong; they must re-read each box to tell whether an exponent or a value is being asked.
number__L04.md.fix: Split the two meanings so 'power' is not asked to mean both. Phrase value-asks as 'Work out 2¹ = [ ]' and exponent-asks as 'The exponent (power) of 2 is [ ]', keeping the wording consistent for which one the box wants.

number__L01.md.why: Every other power in the pack is built by expanding it into repeated multiplication (3 squared = 3 x 3; 2 to the power 4 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2), but the zero-power rule is never explained. You cannot expand 7^0 into a visible multiplication, so a struggling student has nothing to work from and would very likely enter 0 or 7. The counter-intuitive answer (1) makes this gap especially likely to stall them.
number__L01.md.fix: Add a build to this step or the intro, e.g. 'Any number (except 0) to the power 0 equals 1, so 7 to the power 0 = 1.'

number__L01.md.why: The expression is 2^4 - (3 × 2 + 1)^0 × 10. The walk has the student compute the bracket as 7, then the very next step is '1 × 10 =' with no explanation of where the 1 came from. The zero-power rule (any non-zero number to the power 0 = 1, so 7^0 = 1) is never built, stated, or asked. A struggling student who correctly gets 7 in the bracket will be baffled that the next line multiplies 1 (not 7) by 10 — the ^0 step is silently skipped.
number__L01.md.fix: Insert an explaining step between the bracket and the multiply: an intro 'Anything (except 0) raised to the power 0 equals 1, so 7^0 = 1' and/or an ask '7^0 = [box=1]', before 'ask: 1 × 10 = [box=10]'.

number__L01.md.why: Every power in the pack is scaffolded by expanding it into repeated multiplication (e.g. '2 cubed, 2 × 2 × 2', '4 squared, 4 × 4'), but the square root is dropped in raw as '√81 =' with no explanation of what the symbol asks for. A struggling student who has only ever been shown how to square a number has never been taught the inverse operation, so this step presupposes a skill the walk never builds.
number__L01.md.fix: Scaffold the root the same way powers are scaffolded, e.g. '√81 means what number times itself makes 81, 9 × 9 = 81 so √81 =' (box stays NO label — it is a plain number).

number__L01.md.why: The intro builds only ONE sign rule — 'a negative times a negative is positive' — for the (−3) × (−3) step. The very next step, 4 × (−2) = −8, needs the OPPOSITE rule (a positive times a negative is negative), which the walk never states. A struggling student who has just been told neg×neg=positive could reasonably write +8 here. The walk addresses signs for one step and silently omits them for the adjacent one.
number__L01.md.fix: Add the sign rule to this step, e.g. 'Now 4 × (−2): a positive times a negative gives a negative, so the answer is negative.'

graphs__L06.md.why: The sin⁻¹ / cos⁻¹ / tan⁻¹ notation is dropped in cold. Nothing in this lesson builds what inverse trig means; the intro only says 'with the calculator'. A struggling student who has not met the sin⁻¹ button will not know what is being asked. Recurs in gold[1] (cos⁻¹) and gold[2] (tan⁻¹).
graphs__L06.md.fix: Add a bridging line before the box, e.g. 'sin⁻¹(0.5) means: the angle whose sine is 0.5 — press sin⁻¹ (or shift+sin) on the calculator.'

graphs__L06.md.problem: silver[3] (pattern: also silver[2], silver[5], gold[0], gold[2], gold[3])
graphs__L06.md.why: The walk hands over every FORWARD sine/cosine as a ready decimal (e.g. 'sin40° = 0.6428') precisely because a struggling student may not compute them — then abruptly asks the student to evaluate sin⁻¹/cos⁻¹ unaided, with no value supplied and no note about the calculator's inverse (shift/2nd) keys. The skill the answer depends on is the one the walk never builds.
graphs__L06.md.fix: Either supply the inverse result inline, or add a one-line prompt: 'Use sin⁻¹ (shift + sin) on your calculator'

graphs__L06.md.step: The other solution is 180° + 60° = 240°, so the smaller is [box=120]
graphs__L06.md.why: The box wants 120 (computed back in step 2), but the number sitting immediately before the box is the freshly-worked 240. A struggling student will read '...= 240°, so the smaller is ___' and type 240, the last number they saw, not recall the 120 from the previous step. The intended comparison (120 vs 240) is never stated in this sentence.
graphs__L06.md.fix: Restate both candidates in the same sentence: 'The other solution is 180° + 60° = 240°. The smaller of 120° and 240° is ___'.

graphs__L06.md.why: Same trap: the answer 210 comes from step 2, but 330 is the number computed immediately before the box. A weaker student typing the last-seen number will enter 330. The two values being compared (210 and 330) are not both present in this sentence.

number__L02.md.step: Rewrite \(\frac{1}{4}\) over 12. Its new top is [box=3]
number__L02.md.why: The walk jumps from 'the LCD is 12' straight to asking for the new numerator, but never shows the equivalent-fraction scaling method (12 ÷ 4 = 3, then 1 × 3 = 3). Converting a numerator to a new denominator is exactly the step the weakest students fail, and it is presupposed. This same unbuilt skill recurs in every add/subtract walk (bronze 1-3, silver 0-3, gold 0, gold 3).
number__L02.md.fix: Add a bridging line before the ask, e.g. '12 ÷ 4 = 3, so multiply the top by 3: 1 × 3 = ___', mirroring how the mixed-number steps spell out 'top = a × b + c'.

number__L02.md.step: The lowest common denominator of 6 and 8 is [box=24]
number__L02.md.why: No method for finding an LCD is ever built. Where the two bottoms are coprime (4 and 3 → 12) a struggling student can get away with multiplying, but here 6 × 8 = 48, not 24. A student defaulting to 'multiply them' enters the wrong answer and the walk gives no way to know why.
number__L02.md.fix: Add a one-line method, e.g. 'The LCD is the smallest number both 6 and 8 divide into — count 8, 16, 24: 24 works for both. (It is not always the two bottoms multiplied.)'

number__L02.md.step: Rewrite \frac{1}{4} over 12. Its new top is [box=3]
number__L02.md.why: The walk scaffolds simplifying DOWN (it always shows the division, e.g. 'dividing top and bottom by 3. Top: 3 ÷ 3 = ...') but never shows how to scale a fraction UP to a new denominator. It just jumps to 'Its new top is ___'. A struggling student has to independently work out 12 ÷ 4 = 3 then 1 × 3 = 3, a step the walk never models. This same unbuilt 'rewrite over N' step recurs in bronze[2], bronze[7], silver[0], silver[1], silver[4], silver[6], gold[0] and gold[2].
number__L02.md.fix: Add a sub-step showing the multiplier before asking for the new top, e.g. 'To get from 4 to 12 you multiply by 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so the new top is 1 × 3 = ___'.

number__L03.md.step: The greatest 3 decimal place value below 3.48 is?  [box=3.479]
number__L03.md.why: The final step is a bare sentence-fragment question trailing off with 'is?', and it lands the hardest conceptual leap of the pack (that the greatest 3-dp number below 3.48 is 3.479) with no worked reasoning. The opening step 'Write the smallest such x to 2 decimal places' [box=3.47] is also dense: x is defined to 3 dp in the question, so asking for 'the smallest such x to 2 decimal places' reads as contradictory. A struggling student cannot follow this error-interval logic from the wording alone.
number__L03.md.fix: Rewrite step 3 as a full instruction, e.g. 'Any number up to but not including 3.48 truncates to 3.47. Write the largest 3-decimal-place number below 3.48.' Reword step 1 to 'The smallest value that truncates to 3.47 is 3.47 itself — write it.'

number__L03.md.step: 62 sits between 49 and 64, close to 64. Using a calculator, write the root of 62 to 1 decimal place.  [box=7.9]
number__L03.md.why: This is an estimation lesson and the walk builds one method (bounding √62 between 7²=49 and 8²=64), then abandons it and says 'Using a calculator' to reach 7.9. The between-squares reasoning the student just did never actually yields 7.9, so the two halves of the walk contradict each other. A struggling student who followed 'close to 64, so near 8' is left unsure whether to estimate or to calculate.
number__L03.md.fix: Keep one method. Either drop 'Using a calculator' and guide the estimate ('closer to 8 than 7, so try 7.9 — check 7.9×7.9'), or state up front this is a calculator check of the estimate.

number__L03.md.step: intro: The 9 rounds up, so it becomes 10 and carries into the whole number. (appears before) ask: Write the next digit to the right, the decider. [box=5]
number__L03.md.why: The explanation that 'the 9 rounds up and carries' is placed BEFORE the student has been asked to find the decider digit (5). This inverts the rounding routine they are being taught — identify the digit, look at the decider, then decide — so the outcome is announced before its cause. Same out-of-order carry-intro recurs in bronze[5], silver[2] and silver[6], so it will trip the same student repeatedly.
number__L03.md.fix: Move the carry explanation to AFTER the decider box, e.g. ask for the decider (5) first, then intro 'The decider is 5, so the 9 rounds up to 10 and carries into the whole number.'

number__L03.md.step: The perfect square just below 83 is 81, which is [box=9] ... The perfect square just above 83 is 100, which is [box=10]
number__L03.md.why: The phrase '81, which is [9]' never names the operation the box wants — the student has to guess it's asking for a square root. Compare the same pack's gold[4], which explicitly says '4 squared, which is [16]'. Here the operation word is missing, so a struggling student reading '81, which is ___' can't tell what number to type.
number__L03.md.fix: State the operation, e.g. '...is 81, and the square root of 81 is [9]' and '...is 100, and √100 = [10]'.

number__L03.md.step: Check: 25 hundredths is a quarter. Dividing 25 by 25 gives the top of that quarter: 25 ÷ 25 =
number__L03.md.why: The phrasing is opaque and would force a struggling student to re-read several times without following the logic. 'The top of that quarter' means the numerator of 1/4, but that is never said; and using '25 ÷ 25 = 1' as a way to 'check' the answer 0.25 is a contrived leap that has no obvious connection to the 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.25 they just did. The final answer here is 1, which also jars against the 0.25 the whole problem was building to.
number__L03.md.fix: Replace with a plain sanity check, e.g. 'Check: 0.25 is the same as one quarter. A quarter of 4 is 1, so type' [box=1] — or drop this check entirely and confirm 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.25 directly.

number__L03.md.step: Check: 25 hundredths is a quarter. Dividing 25 by 25 gives the top of that quarter: 25 ÷ 25 = [box=1]

The check-logic (why dividing 25 by 25 verifies 0.25 = a quarter) is never explained, so the student re-reads it and still has no idea what is being confirmed. It reads as a non-sequitur bolted onto a correct answer.
number__L03.md.fix: Rewrite the check plainly, e.g. 'Check: 0.25 is the same as one quarter (1/4), which is a sensible size. As a fraction of 1, that quarter has 1 on top: 25 ÷ 25 = [box=1].' Drop the 'top of that quarter' phrasing.
